newsitem.title: RWANDA: U.N. envoy seeks access to refugees in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy seeks access to refugees in Zaire.

text.p: A U.N. refugee agency envoy said after talks with Rwandan military strongman Paul Kagame on Tuesday his agency was seeking access to more than a million refugees scattered or trapped by fighting in eastern Zaire.

Assistant High Commissioner for Refugees Sergio Vieira de Mello said he had held fruitful talks on the fighting and plight of refugees with Major-General Kagame, who is vice-president and defence minister of Rwanda.
"The discussions we held were a first step towards seeking access to the refugees in eastern Zaire," he told reporters.
"There is a consensus that the refugees must return home. This whole episode has lasted too long and there is more suffering for the refugees.
"We are urgently trying to reach the refugees and my meetings in Kigali and Kinshasa on Wednesday are aimed at reaching this goal," said the special envoy before leaving for Kinshasa.
Officials said an Organisation of African Unity (OAU) peace mission led by assistant Secretary-General Anatole Tiendrebeogo would also meet Kagame on Tuesday in Rwanda's capital.
The OAU wants a framework for dialogue between warring sides to prevent the war from spreading in the giant African country.

"There is evidence that a lot of refugees would like to come back home. So we need to get in there (eastern Zaire) and be able to help repatriate them back home," said Paul Stromberg, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
Diplomats in Kigali said the meetings with Kagame were significant because he controls Rwanda's 54,000-strong, Tutsi-dominated army as the chairman of the high command.
"It is far more useful to meet and hold talks with Kagame on the plight of refugees than to hold conferences far away from the region. He is the key to what Rwanda does next," a diplomat said.
African leaders met in the Kenyan capital Nairobi on Tuesday to discuss the fighting between Zaire's army and Tutsi rebels and the plight of more than a million refugees caught in the war zone.
Zaire accuses Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda of backing the rebels, who in the past two weeks have seized much of eastern Zaire and a string of border cities and towns in Africa's newest civil war.
The war erupted two weeks ago when local Zairean authorities in Bukavu tried to expel ethnic Banyamulenge Tutsis from Zaire back to Rwanda -- a land they left as long ago as 200 years ago.
On Monday night, Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu made a special appeal to Rwandan refugees to return and help rebuild their country and promised equality and fairness.
Rwanda like neighbouring Burundi is divided between minority Tutsis and majority Hutus. In both countries, Tutsi-dominated armies hold sway.

Refugees have been on the road since fighting erupted in eastern Zaire and aid agencies are warning of a humanitarian disaster unless aid reached them or corridors were opened to enable them return home.
Many Hutu refugees refuse to return home for fear of reprisals for their role in the 1994 genocide of up to a million Tutsis in Rwanda and have headed deeper into Zaire.
